'''''Scutellaria galericulata''''', the '''common skullcap''', '''marsh skullcap'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=SCGA4|taxon=Scutellaria galericulata|access-date=8 November 2015}}</ref> or '''hooded skullcap''', is a hardy [[perennial plant|perennial]] [[herb]] native to northern areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, Asia, and almost all of Canada. It is a member of the [[Lamiaceae|mint family]]. The form is upright and is usually 20-45 centimeters in height,<ref name="plant-identification.co.uk">{{Cite web|url=http://www.plant-identification.co.uk/skye/labiatae/scutellaria-galericulata.htm|title=''Scutellaria galericulata''|access-date=2007-04-24|archive-date=2008-07-31|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080731061922/http://www.plant-identification.co.uk/skye/labiatae/scutellaria-galericulata.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> sometimes reaching up to 80 cm.<ref>[http://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?4745,4892,4898 Jepson Manual Treatment]</ref> It is a [[Wetland|wetland-loving]] species and grows along [[fen]]s and shorelines. The blue flowers are 1 to 2 centimeters long. The flowers are in pairs and are all on the same side of the stem. The flowers do not appear at the top of the stem.

The plant is native to many parts of the world and, as such, is known by a variety of names. The Latin ''galericulata'' means "hooded", relating to the length of the flower's tube being much longer than the [[sepal|calyx]].<ref name="plant-identification.co.uk"/> The variation ''epilobiifolia'' translates as ''leaves like willow-herb'', and refers to the slightly serrated long thin leaves which look similar to those of the genus ''[[Epilobium]]''.

==Medicinal uses==
{{more medical citations needed|section|date=September 2012}}
The genus ''[[Scutellaria]]'' has numerous medicinal uses and various species of skullcap are used in the same way. The traditional uses of common skullcap should not be confused with those of other Skullcaps as there are over 200 different species of Skullcap and they are not all used in the same way. [[Scutellaria lateriflora|Blue skullcap]] (''S. lateriflora'') is accepted as the "skullcap" used in traditional [[North America]]n medicine, however common skullcap shares many of the same active chemicals and is used as a substitute in Britain and Europe.<ref name="Wills">R. B. H. Wills, D.L. Stuart, ''Generation of High Quality Australian Skullcap Products'', 2004, {{ISBN|0-642-58730-2}}, {{ISSN|1440-6845}} http://www.rirdc.gov.au/reports/EOI/04-020.pdf</ref> Common skullcap (''S. galericulata'') is also often used in the same way as [[Scutellaria canescens|Western skullcap]] (''S. canescens'') and [[Scutellaria cordifolia|Southern skullcap]] (''S. cordifolia''), all of which are genetically similar.<ref>P. Wolfson, MD, and D. L. Hoffmann, FNIMH, Alternative Therapies, Mar/Apr 2003, Vol. 9, No. 2 75.</ref>

Blue skullcap and common skullcap are mainly known for their traditional use as mild [[anxiolytic]]s in the form of [[herbal tea]]s, tablets, capsules, dried leaf for smoking and oral liquid preparations, often in combination with other medicinal herbs.{{citation needed|date=September 2012}} The aqueous extract of the flowering parts have been traditionally used by [[Indigenous peoples of the Americas|Native Americans]] as a nerve tonic and for its [[sedative]] and [[diuretic]] properties.<ref>Millspaugh, C. F. American Medicinal Plants; Dover Publications: New York, 1974; pp 469-472</ref>
